editorials.title: Hog in the limelight: On Assam’s pygmy hog programme
editorials.passage:
The decline of the pygmy hog — the sole surviving species of the genus Porcula and the world’s smallest wild suid — is a narrative about the decline of India’s alluvial floodplains. The pygmy hog depends significantly on dense grasslands to feed, conceal itself, and reproduce, so distress among these animals is an indicator of the floodplain suffering degradation. Protecting the pygmy hog can also extend protections to threatened species such as the Bengal florican, hispid hare, hog deer, and greater one-horned rhinoceros. The Assam government was recently right to laud the efforts of a captive breeding programme that increased the pygmy hog population in the State 32-fold in the last three decades. Breeding from a small founder stock while preventing diseases — suids are highly susceptible to swine diseases — and inbreeding requires conservationists to track pedigree, follow biosafety protocols, and condition individuals before release. That said, the species’ survival in the wild depends on the survival of specific ecosystems, and the latter remains a work in progress. The pygmy hog was believed to be extinct by the mid-20th century as floodplains were converted for farms, tea plantations, and flood control infrastructure and were degraded by invasive plants and altered flood cycles, with the unscientific burning of grasslands further fragmenting habitats. A few individuals were rediscovered in 1971, prompting one conservation effort. The current efforts are due to the Pygmy Hog Conservation Programme from 1995.

Even now, the difficulty of spotting and counting these animals means that it is hard to say how many exist in the wild; per the Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, there were some 250 individuals in early 2025, with the last surviving natural population in the Panbari grasslands area of the Manas National Park. Since they continue to be threatened, the captive individuals form the insurance group, but even so, the group’s long-term evolutionary fitness is still not guaranteed. Researchers are also alert to the accumulation of harmful gene variants in the population and low genetic diversity, and thus look forward to the pygmy hog’s natural habitats being restored. Alluvial floodplains are dynamic ecosystems; in addition to threats such as land conversion, efforts to ‘save’ them, such as widespread dry-season fires, can still destroy the dense cover the pygmy hog needs. On the other hand, suppressing ecological processes can leave trees and shrubs to turn grassland into woodland. Given the plan to increase the wild pygmy hog population to 300 by 2040, Assam needs to revert the fragmentation of its protected grasslands, especially in Rupahi and Kanchanbari, and to restore buffer zones around the Manas and Orang National Parks and the Sonai Rupai Wildlife Sanctuary.

editorials.title: Currency conundrum: On the BRICS New Delhi Declaration
editorials.passage:
The BRICS New Delhi Declaration shows that progress in enhancing local currency trade has been incremental. The paragraph pertaining to local currency trade acknowledges the efforts of various task forces and committees but falls short of offering any concrete proposals. Recently, the Commerce Ministry indicated that India’s rupee trade with its BRICS partners was limited, with only the UAE and Russia engaged in it. Even those volumes are relatively small. Until recently, Russia had struggled to dispose of the rupees it was accumulating from its exports to India. Some avenues have now opened, with Russia being forced to import petroleum products from India due to Ukraine’s attacks. But that is a trickle. Another option is to treat any BRICS currency as ‘local’. India has already been using the UAE Dirham to pay for Russian oil. However, the latest Declaration’s mention of promoting BRICS local currency trade “while respecting national priorities and acknowledging that there is no one-size-fits-all approach” is telling. Clearly, there are some intra-BRICS issues that need to be addressed. The deliberations are not public, but it would not be surprising if it was India that had emphasised national priorities and raised problems with a “one-size-fits-all” approach. Local currency trade involves several strategic considerations for India.

On the one hand, India would prefer to continue being paid for its exports in dollars. A depreciating rupee ensures that every dollar paid to India results in a higher amount of rupees. As a country looking to boost exports, India would want to retain this advantage. On the other hand, India is also a major importer and would like to pay in relatively cheaper local currencies. It will eventually have to choose. Then there is the fact that China accounts for about two-thirds of all BRICS exports. BRICS local currency trade will largely be trade in the yuan. Relations with China might be thawing now, but India would still be loath to conduct its business in the yuan. It is also important to distinguish between local currency trade and a BRICS currency. While India has so far been cautiously supportive of the former, it has been vocal in opposing a BRICS currency, largely because of China’s likely dominance of such a currency. Then there is U.S. President Donald Trump’s threat of 100% tariffs on countries adopting a BRICS currency. India has displayed a pragmatic approach to dealing with Mr. Trump, and it will not court such tariff threats lightly. Countries such as Iran and Russia have pressing reasons to move away from the dollar. So far, India does not have a convincing enough one, and the New Delhi Declaration reflects that.

editorials.title: Strengthen global net to catch animal smugglers
editorials.passage: More than a week after the rescue of five baby orangutans from Odisha’s Balasore district, the whodunit continues to baffle the nation. The Wildlife Crime Control Bureau, a central agency, and the state’s special task force are on the job. But very little has surfaced in terms of clues to trace the apes’ route from their home in the rainforests of Indonesia and Malaysia to an alien land far away. It appears to be a smuggling operation gone wrong, with traffickers dumping the babies near the eastern coast. Orangutan smuggling is not new in India. A spate of seizures in Mizoram, Assam and Maharashtra in recent years shows that the illegal trade uses the Myanmar-Thailand-Bangladesh route to feed demand in the country. It’s possible that with the enforcement agencies focused on known smuggling corridors in the Northeast, the traffickers were trying a new route through Odisha.The investigation requires the support of international agencies working against wildlife trafficking. Rehabilitating the baby apes is also desirable, but their lineage must be established and the primates repatriated as per UNEP’s Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species. Orangutans are facing the scourge of expanding palm plantations and climate change eroding their natural habitats. Yet home is where they belong, not in our zoos..Their smuggling, meanwhile, must raise an alarm for Indian authorities. The Directorate of Revenue Intelligence’s 2024-25 report noted that lucrative profits of exotic pet trade is a key driver of wildlife smuggling in the country. The worldwide trade is billed at a massive $20 billion, whereas seizure data for 2015-21 places South Asia at 9 percent of the global total. India also acts as a source for trade in pangolin scales, elephant tusks, tiger and leopard skins as well as turtles, while serving as a transit space for other exotic species. Much of the trade is contracted online. The UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2024 report cited a case where a trafficker in Indonesia had placed bids for tigers and star tortoises to be delivered in Thailand, with the network spanning India, Pakistan and Malaysia operating through social media platforms. It’s evident that India cannot fight this illicit global trade on its own. editorials.title: With the US weaponising the final frontier, space treaty needs an update
editorials.passage: In a move that could trigger a perilous space-based arms race, the US on Monday admitted to deploying “on-orbit space control weapons”. While the nature of weapons installed remained classified in the US air force secretary’s announcement, experts warned it could take weapons of mass destruction literally to the next frontier.The deployment threatens the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, signed by at least 118 countries including India, the US, China and Russia (as part of the erstwhile Soviet Union). It bans WMDs in space and prohibits militarisation of celestial bodies, including building military bases and conducting weapons tests. It, however, does not ban conventional systems or counter-space technologies in low-Earth orbits. But the ‘known unknown’ of the weapons deployed begs the question: how far are we from a nuclear arms race in space?Several countries have for long been capable of a space arms race. In January 1975, the Soviet Union remotely fired 20 shells from the Salyut-3 space station. China and India have destroyed their own defunct satellites using missiles fired from the ground in 2007 and 2019, respectively. None of this, however, violated the 1967 treaty. China and Russia have also developed space-based capabilities for electronic warfare..The US deployment is not an overnight decision. In January 2001, the US Space Commission headed by Donald Rumsfeld, then the defence secretary, recommended a space policy to empower the US President with “the option to deploy weapons in space to deter threats to, and, if necessary, defend against attacks on US interests”. The following year, the US’s withdrawal from the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty allowed it to pursue space-based missile defence. Those early moves culminated in Donald Trump creating the US Space Force in 2019 during his first term as President. So, the US plan to weaponise space has been in the making for at least a quarter century.Defending mankind from incoming comets, meteors or asteroids using weapons is one thing—a technology tested by the European Space Agency’s 2014 Rosetta mission. But justifying weapons in space by citing threats from unnamed “adversaries” is nothing short of threatening the planet while pursuing narrow national security. Several countries’ move towards commercial mineral extraction in space is also weakening the 1967 treaty’s bar against national appropriation of celestial resources. It’s time to update it keeping mankind’s safety firmly in view..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

editorials.title: Quick Take | Vocal for locals
editorials.passage: Deborah Thiagarajan has brought attention to an oft-ignored aspect of tourism—that locals of modest means often do not get to earn from it. Speaking at TNIE’s Tourism Summit, the founder-director of DakshinaChitra Heritage Museum also pointed to young visitors’ thirst for experiences rather than exhibits. Among the initiatives that serve both needs, an NGO’s work in Madhya Pradesh stands out. A year before Airbnb took off, Friends of Orchha started as a community-run homestay in a poorer part of the historic town. The NGO attracted visitors online, constructed pukka rooms and toilets in hutments, and introduced the hosts to the visitors. As the years passed, the hosts automatically paid off the NGO and started running the show themselves. editorials.title: Vanishing Ground ~ II
editorials.passage:
Begin with an older vocabulary for the duty. In the third chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that even one who has nothing personal left to gain should still act loka-sangraham evapi sampashyan ~ with an eye to the holding-together of the world (3.20, and again at 3.25). Lokasangraha is not private charity or personal merit; it is the maintenance of the social and moral order, the labour of keeping a habitable world so that others are not driven, by neglect, onto the path of ruin. 

Sankara, in his commentary, reads it as the duty of the wise and the powerful to keep society from sliding into disorder; Radhakrishnan renders it simply as the maintenance of the world order. The concept is, in a precise sense, a thread ~ a terse imperative that means little until it is unspooled into the particular duties of a particular office, in the way a sutra means little until its commentary unfolds it. In a republic that office is the State’s, and the thread reaches it as an old form of rajadharma. A polity that can survey every receding metre of its shoreline, as this one has, and still leave the people who stood on it without status has measured the land and forgotten the citizen. 

The point is not merely homiletic, for the Constitution already contains the commentary the thread requires. Article 21’s guarantee of life has, for four decades, been read to mean far more than survival. In Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi (1981), the Supreme Court, through Justice Bhagwati, held that it means the right to live with human dignity, including the bare necessaries such as adequate food, clothing and shelter; in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation (1985), that it embraces the right to livelihood, since to strip a person of the means of living is to deprive them of life itself; in Chameli Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (1996), that the right to shelter is a component of the right to life; and in Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991), that it includes the enjoyment of pollutionfree water and air. 

Each of these cases concerned a person facing the deliberate hand of the State, not the slow hand of the sea. Then, in March 2024, in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, a bench led by the Chief Justice took the step that makes the rest cohere: reading Articles 14 and 21 together with the Constitution’s environmental directives, it recognised a distinct right against the adverse effects of climate change. The logic now travels the whole distance. If eviction by a municipality engages Article 21, and the climate itself is a recognised source of constitutional injury, then the citizen whose home is erased by an erosion the State has measured and failed to plan against does not need a new right invented for her. She already has one. What she lacks is its machinery. 

And a right without machinery is a consolation, not a remedy. The failure is one of fit as much as of will. The Disaster Management Act answers the sudden event, not the slow one; and the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act of 2013 ~ India’s most generous resettlement statute ~ does not reach the delta’s displaced at all, for it is triggered by the State’s acquisition of land for a public purpose, and the sea acquires nothing the State can be made to compensate. 

A principle at the centre is inert until someone supplies its commentary in language that can actually be enforced. What India lacks, and must draft, is a statutory Climate Displacement and Resettlement Framework ~ the bhashya, one might say, that the constitutional principle has been waiting on. It would begin with definitional clarity: who counts as an internally displaced climate migrant, on what threshold of loss, established by what evidence, so that entitlement does not turn on which cyclone reached the evening news, and so that slow erosion, salinisation and sea-level rise are named alongside the storm. 

It would fix a compensation structure keyed not to the market price of drowned land, which is by definition worthless, but to the cost of a dignified restart, and would confront directly the question the land-acquisition law evades ~ how a title survives the plot that bore it. It would guarantee resettlement rights: to serviced land, to the restoration of livelihood, to the keeping-together of a community rather than its scattering across unfamiliar districts. And it would name a single authority, sitting between the disaster machinery and the revenue administration, answerable for registration, risk-mapping and delivery, so that the displaced have someone to hold to account rather than a queue to join. 

None of this is visionary; the models exist, and one of them shares the delta. In 2021 Bangladesh adopted a National Strategy on Internal Displacement Management, built around three phases ~ prevention before displacement, protection during it, and durable solutions after ~ for the very population that the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta produces on both sides of the border. Further afield, the African Union’s Kampala Convention, in force since 2012, was the first binding regional treaty to oblige states to protect the internally displaced, disaster among the recognised causes. 


India, which has urged such protections in international forums, would be following a path already marked rather than breaking a new one. None of this demands the invention of a new fundamental right; the Court has supplied that. It asks Parliament to give the right its instruments ~ to write the commentary the Constitution has been left waiting on, and that two lapsed Bills already sketched. That is a smaller task than it sounds, and a more urgent one, for the delta will not wait on the drafting. Every monsoon that passes without such a framework is another season in which citizens are made stateless within their own state, counted in the census yet absent from the statute book. 

The Gita’s instruction to the powerful was to act for the holding-together of the world; the Constitution’s promise, now including a right against the very climate that is unmaking the delta, was that no life within its borders would be lived without dignity. The Sundarbans is where those two commitments are being tested against the water, and the water, as the 4,000 of Ghoramara have learned, keeps its own schedule. The question is no longer whether the tide will take more of Bengal’s edge. It is whether the law will still be looking the other way when it does. 

(The writer is a practising Chartered Accountant and a Vedantic Scholar. He can be reached at kannan@cakt.in)

editorials.title: Putting a meter on our best public rail
editorials.passage:
For most Indians, paying through UPI has felt like paying with nothing at all. Scan, enter the PIN, done. For a slice of transactions, that is about to change. From October 15, merchants receiving UPI payments above Rs 2,000 will pay a merchant discount rate, or MDR, of 0.4 per cent. A Rs 3,000 bill will cost the shopkeeper Rs 12. A Rs 50,000 purchase will cost Rs 200. At Rs 75,000 and above, the charge stops rising at Rs 300. The ground was prepared on September 14, when the Finance Ministry issued a notification under Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. 

It named RuPay debit cards and UPI payments up to Rs 2,000 as modes on which no bank or system provider may impose a charge, directly or indirectly, on the person paying or the person being paid. A day later, the UPI and Services Steering Committee, led by the National Payments Corporation of India, spelt out what happens above that line. The fine print is narrower than the headlines. Transfers between individuals stay free, whatever the amount. Small vendors classified as P2PM, those receiving up to Rs 1 lakh a month through UPI, are exempt. Recurring AutoPay mandates carry no prescribed MDR. 

Some categories, including railways, telecom, insurance, fuel and utilities, will pay a flat Rs 5 on payments above Rs 2,000, while capital-market transactions will attract 0.02 per cent, also capped at Rs 300. The ministry says 96 per cent of merchant transactions will remain free. The reasoning deserves a fair hearing. In July 2026 alone, UPI processed about 2,366 crore transactions worth roughly Rs 29.9 lakh crore, according to government figures. A system of that size is no longer a convenience. It is critical national infrastructure, and it needs servers, fraud detection, authentication, cybersecurity and constant upgrades. 

Since January 2020, when MDR on UPI was scrapped to encourage digital payments, banks and payment apps have earned little from the basic merchant transaction, and government subsidies have filled part of the gap. The Finance Minister has pointed to Australia, Brazil, China, Indonesia, South Korea, Singapore, Thailand and the United States, where digital payments carry a cost. The logic is simple enough: leave the tea stall and the vegetable vendor alone, and recover something from larger commercial payments. No sensible person believes UPI costs nothing to run. 

The trouble lies elsewhere. The debate has fixed on one number: the cost of processing a single UPI transaction. The more useful number is the cost of making that same payment the old way. Imagine a commuter who used to spend Rs 1,500 a month on a crowded bus. He switches to the metro, pays Rs 800 and gets a better ride. Then he starts complaining about the Rs 800. He is staring at the bill and ignoring the saving. Our policy conversation is in much the same place. Cash is expensive in ways that never appear on NPCI's books. Notes must be printed, transported, guarded and loaded into ATMs, then counted and reconciled. Taxes go unpaid because cash leaves no trail. 

Welfare leaks before it reaches the people it was meant for. Every payment shifted from cash to UPI trims that bill, and most of the saving goes to the state and the wider economy, not to the person scanning the code. UPI has most of the features economists associate with a public good. It is open and interoperable, so any bank or app can connect, and one person's use takes nothing away from another's. Once the rails exist, each additional transaction costs very little. The network becomes more valuable with every new user and merchant. A small vendor needs a printed QR code, not a card machine. Its digital record draws economic activity into the formal system. Entrepreneurs build lending, savings and commerce products on top of it. 

And it gives India a domestic payments backbone that does not depend on private international networks. A large part of this value goes to people who are not party to the transaction. Economists call that a positive externality, and it changes the arithmetic. UPI cannot be judged on private cost against private revenue. It has to be judged on social benefit against social cost. Framed that way, the real question is not who is subsidising UPI. It is why we would put a toll on infrastructure whose returns spread so far beyond any single payment. The promise that consumers will not bear the fee assumes merchants will quietly absorb it. Indian retail seldom works like that. Anyone who has been asked for an extra 2 per cent to pay by credit card knows how quickly a cost reaches the customer. 

Expect "UPI charges" at electronics stores, furniture showrooms, clinics and repair workshops, or a polite suggestion to pay in cash instead. A 0.4 per cent fee is small. It may still be enough to push a jeweller or a contractor back towards cash, which is precisely the habit UPI was meant to break. The 96 per cent figure also reassures more than it should. It counts transactions, not money. Payments above Rs 2,000 are fewer in number, but they are likely to account for a far larger share of value, and they are the payments where a digital trail matters most for tax collection. There is a political miscalculation here too. UPI is one of the few public systems that works well for nearly everyone, and people know it. 

Opening the door to charges, however carefully fenced, signals that the free era is ending. Once a fee exists, raising it later needs only a committee meeting, not an act of Parliament. None of this means the system should be starved of money. If UPI needs dedicated funding for security and resilience, the Budget should provide it openly, as core infrastructure, and weigh it against the cash-handling costs UPI removes. The amount is modest compared with what the state spends elsewhere each year. 

Banks and payment apps can also be allowed to earn from services built on the rail, such as credit, analytics and merchant tools, rather than from the rail itself. And if the MDR stays, the government should publish what it raises, show where the money goes, and review the fee after a year against data on cash usage. India achieved something rare with UPI. It built public payments infrastructure that the rest of the world now studies. The advantage was never only the technology. It was that using it cost almost nothing. That is worth protecting, even if protecting it has a price. 

(The writer is a tech and social entrepreneur, public policy commentator and columnist)

editorials.title: Delhi, Beijing must join hands for global peace
editorials.passage:
The bilateral meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit 2026 in New Delhi sent a powerful and positive message of diplomatic revival and pragmatic engagement to the world. Coming as a significant step forward in a gradual thaw since the 2020 border standoffs, the dialogue signalled that the world's two most populous nations are actively prioritizing "partners over rivals" to stabilize their vast geopolitical and economic relationship. 

By reaching a core consensus on mutual cooperation, the leaders underscored that peace and tranquillity along the border remain the essential foundation for moving forward, while agreeing to use political wisdom to manage specific differences. Furthermore, their commitment to addressing structural trade imbalances, reviving people-to-people exchanges, and cooperating on global platforms sent a reassuring signal of stability to the Global South and the wider international order during a period of intense global economic uncertainty. The contemporary global order is fractured by two devastating, overlapping conflicts: the Russia-Ukraine war and the US-Iran war. 

These conflicts are no longer regional disputes; they have mutated into systemic crises threatening global energy supplies, economic stability, and international security. As the pre- eminent economic powerhouses and demographic giants of Asia, India and China hold a unique, historically significant obligation to lead the world toward peace. While bilateral friction has long defined their relationship, the existential threats of these dual wars dictate that Beijing and New Delhi must put aside their border disputes to forge a joint diplomatic front. 

By leveraging their collective strategic autonomy, economic clout, and shared regional platforms like BRICS and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), India and China can - and must - intervene to end these endless hostilities. The most immediate and pragmatic reason for Sino-Indian cooperation is the profound threats these wars pose to their domestic economic growth. China is the world's largest crude importer, drawing roughly half of its supply from the Middle East. The US-Iran war directly imperils the Strait of Hormuz, a critical choke point through which Asian energy lifelines flow. Similarly, India's rapid development relies heavily on stable, affordable energy. 

While India has cushioned its economy by purchasing discounted Russian oil amid the Ukraine war, an uncontained conflict in the Middle East coupled with persistent Western sanctions severely disrupts maritime trade and fuels runaway inflation. If major Asian powers can speak with one voice, the rest of the world will listen. Renowned economist Jeffrey Sachs noted that a combined demand from India and China to "end the war" holds unparalleled weight. If the fighting continues, the prolonged economic costs will be catastrophically absorbed by Asia. The dual wars have accelerated a highly volatile realignment of global powers, forcing both Beijing and New Delhi into uncomfortable diplomatic tightropes. 

For India, the prolonged Russia-Ukraine war has pushed its historical partner, Moscow, into an asymmetrical economic and political dependence on Beijing. This shifts the balance of power in Asia, complicating India's security landscape. Concurrently, Washington's aggressive stances and transactional policies - such as imposing tariffs on Indian exports over Russian oil ties - expose the limits of relying solely on Western alliances. For China, a protracted war involving the United States in the Middle East may temporarily distract Washington, but it risks a catastrophic global escalation that undermines Beijing's long-term economic integration projects. By working together, India and China can neutralise the pressure to "choose sides". 

A united Asian consensus would provide a buffer against the destabilising actions of an unpredictable United States and a desperate Russia, preserving the multipolar world that both Asian powers desire. India and China possess the exact diplomatic architecture needed to broker peace, yet they underutilized it due to mutual distrust. As key members of the SCO and the expanded BRICS bloc, they sit at the same table as the primary combatants and their closest allies. Iran and Russia are both members of these blocks, making them uniquely receptive to Asian diplomacy. 

Currently, differences between India and China have hamstrung these institutions from forging a unified stance on the West Asia crisis. If Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping synchronise their strategies, they can transform BRICS and the SCO from passive talking shops into powerful conflict-resolution mechanisms. They can collectively pressure Moscow to accept a realistic exit strategy in Ukraine and leverage their deep ties with Tehran to facilitate a ceasefire with the US and Israel. The solution to the modern world's geopolitical fires cannot be found on the battlefield. As Prime Minister Modi aptly remarked at the SCO Summit, humanity must move "from endless war to the end of war." 

Neither the United States nor Russia can unilaterally dictate a peaceful global order anymore. For India and China, cooperation is no longer an idealistic choice; it is an absolute strategic necessity. By leveraging China’s unparalleled economic leverage over Moscow and Tehran alongside India’s robust diplomatic credibility with both the West and the Global South, these two Asian titans can stop the global slide into total war. In doing so, they will not only protect their own economic futures but will permanently secure their status as the rightful, responsible leaders of the 21st century. India and China do not need to agree on every geopolitical issue to recognize a shared fire when it burns near their homes. 

India and China must unite their diplomatic influence to demand an end to the US-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars because these ongoing conflicts severely threaten both nations' energy security and economic stability. As global heavyweights, New Delhi and Beijing possess the collective economic and political weight to push warring parties toward the negotiating table. Working together is no longer just a diplomatic choice; it is an urgent necessity for Asian and global survival. Cooperation on global peace can also help India and China improve their own bilateral relations. As both nations work to stabilize their border regions and maintain economic growth, partnering for global stability offers a clear path forward. 

The writer, a retired IFS officer, served as India’s Ambassador to Kuwait and Morocco and as ConsulGeneral in New York.

editorials.title: Himalayan Bill
editorials.passage:
India has long treated the Himalayas as scenery, frontier and source of water. It now needs to treat the majestic mountains as something more consequential: critical economic infrastructure. The distinction matters because a deteriorating mountain ecosystem can impose costs far beyond the states in which the damage occurs. Glaciers across the Himalayan region are losing mass at an accelerating rate. That does not translate into a simple story of rivers running dry tomorrow. The immediate problem can be the opposite: unstable slopes, expanding glacial lakes and sudden floods. 

The long-term danger is more profound. Once glaciers lose mass, the rivers they feed will increasingly become dependent on increasingly erratic snowfall and rainfall. For India, this is an economic problem disguised as a geographical one. Himalayan water supports agriculture, hydropower, tourism and the lives of hundreds of millions of people. Wheat and rice cultivation in the plains, electricity generation in mountain states and the enormous pilgrimage economy all depend, directly or indirectly, on the stability of this water system. Any serious disruption will therefore be reflected in food prices, electricity costs, infrastructure losses and public finances. 

The warning signs are already visible. The 2021 Uttarakhand disaster and the 2023 Sikkim glacial lake outburst showed how quickly a mountain hazard can become a national infrastructure crisis. Roads, bridges and hydropower installations are often concentrated in narrow valleys precisely where floods and landslides can be most destructive. Yet India's response remains too fragmented. Disaster management authorities prepare for disasters; environmental agencies monitor ecosystems; infrastructure ministries build roads and power projects; tourism departments pursue visitor numbers. The Himalayas do not operate according to these bureaucratic divisions. A road, dam or tourist settlement alters the risk faced by everything downstream. 

The monitoring deficit is particularly troubling. Thousands of glaciers exist across the wider Himalayan-Karakoram system, but only a tiny fraction receive sustained, detailed observation. Governments cannot manage hazards they cannot see developing. Satellite surveillance, ground sensors, glacial-lake mapping and shared hydrological data should therefore be treated as essential infrastructure, not specialist scientific projects. There is also a relatively neglected opportunity. Black carbon from combustion sources, including pollution generated in the plains, contributes significantly to accelerated melting. Reducing soot emissions will not solve climate change, but it is one area where regional action can produce relatively direct benefits for the Himalayas. 

Money must follow the risk. Mountain states should not be left to finance the protection of an ecological system whose economic benefits flow across India. National investment in resilient infrastructure, early-warning systems and ecosystem protection is justified precisely because the beneficiaries are national. And the Himalayas cannot be governed through national boundaries alone. Rivers, glaciers and atmospheric pollution cross borders. India, Nepal, Bhutan, Pakistan and China have different interests and political relationships, but none can make the mountain system obey a passport. The choice is therefore not between development and environmental protection. It is between paying deliberately for resilience now or paying unpredictably for Himalayan instability later. India should recognise which option is cheaper.

editorials.title: Fraying Union
editorials.passage:
Britain’s constitutional argument has entered a more serious phase. The question is no longer simply whether Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland can demand greater autonomy from Westminster. It is whether the United Kingdom can continue to function as a political union when increasingly influential forces within three of its four nations question the permanence of that union. 

The meeting of John Swinney, Scotland’s First Minister and leader of the Scottish National Party; Rhun ap Iorwerth, Wales’s First Minister and leader of the pro-independence Plaid Cymru; and Michelle O’Neill, Northern Ireland’s First Minister and a senior Sinn Féin leader, is significant because all three now head devolved governments whose governing parties favour breaking, in different ways, with the United Kingdom. That does not make the dissolution of the UK inevitable. Indeed, the obstacles remain formidable. Scotland voted against independence in 2014, and the UK government has resisted another referendum. 

Northern Ireland has a distinct constitutional framework under the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, which provides for a border poll under specified circumstances. Wales is further behind, with Plaid Cymru itself previously ruling out an independence referendum during the current Senedd term. But the political significance lies elsewhere. For decades, the Union could be presented as the settled constitutional framework within which disagreements about taxation, public services and devolution were conducted. That assumption is weakening. Independence is increasingly becoming part of mainstream political debate rather than a peripheral nationalist demand. Westminster should therefore be careful about treating these developments as merely the work of separatist politicians. The deeper problem may be one of institutional legitimacy. 

Devolution was intended to accommodate national identities within the United Kingdom, but it also created powerful democratic institutions capable of articulating demands that Westminster cannot permanently ignore. The economic argument will be at least as important as the constitutional one. Independence requires credible answers about public finances, trade, currency, debt, energy and social security. Nationalist governments cannot win lasting public support merely by invoking identity. Equally, Westminster cannot defend the Union simply by warning of economic uncertainty. Both sides will eventually have to demonstrate that their preferred constitutional arrangement can deliver prosperity and effective government. The irony is that the Union’s future may depend less on nationalist rhetoric than on Westminster’s response. 

A confident Union would seek to persuade Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland that remaining within it serves their interests while respecting their democratic identities. A defensive Westminster that regards every demand for greater autonomy as an existential threat could instead reinforce the very grievance on which separatism feeds. Britain is not necessarily approaching disintegration. But its constitutional settlement is no longer politically settled. The choice before Westminster is increasingly stark: renew the Union through consent and accommodation, or risk discovering that a union preserved by refusal may eventually become a union preserved in name alone.

editorials.title: Moral mooring
editorials.passage:
The story of the Indian Constitution is often narrated through institutions, debates, and legal provisions. We repeatedly speak of the Constituent Assembly debates, fundamental rights, federalism, parliamentary democracy, and judicial review. Yet Constitutions are never merely legal documents; they are repositories of the moral imagination as well. Behind every constitutional text lies a philosophy of human beings, society, and power.

India's Constitution emerged from a remarkable sangam (confluence) of intellectual traditions. The anti-colonial struggle, liberal constitutionalism, socialist ideas, the experience of social reform movements, and the lived realities of an unequal society left their imprint upon it. Among these influences, one of the most profound, though not always sufficiently appreciated and acknowledged, was the philosophical legacy of Gautama Buddha. The Buddha's emphasis on reason, compassion, equality and ethical responsibility found two of its most significant modern interpreters in B.R. Ambedkar and Jawaharlal Nehru. Their engagements with Buddhism differed in emphasis and purpose; yet together, they endowed India's constitutional democracy with a distinctive moral vocabulary.

Neither Ambedkar nor Nehru approached the Buddha merely as the founder of a religion but they encountered him essentially as a philosopher of human freedom. Both recognised that the Buddha had inaugurated one of the earliest traditions of rational inquiry in India — a tradition that challenged inherited authority, questioned ritual hierarchy, and insisted that truth must withstand the scrutiny of reason and experience. The Buddha's famous exhortation in the Kalama Sutta , not to accept an idea merely because it is ancient, sanctioned by scripture or endorsed by authority, resonated deeply with the democratic temperament. It affirmed the dignity of individual judgment because democracy, after all, begins not only with the right to vote but also with the recognition that every individual possesses the moral capacity to think, question and decide.

Nehru found this aspect of Buddhism particularly compelling and throughout his writings, especially in The Discovery of India and in Glimpses of World History , he returned repeatedly to the Buddha as one of the greatest representatives of India's rational and humanistic civilisation. The Buddha rejected dogma without descending into cynicism; he cultivated compassion without abandoning reason. Nehru admired the Buddha because he encouraged intellectual humility.

For Nehru, this inheritance was indispensable to the making of modern India. A democratic republic required more than periodic elections. It required citizens capable of critical thought, tolerance, and self-restraint. It demanded what Nehru famously described as the "scientific temper", a disposition to examine evidence, question prejudice, and remain open to revision. In many respects, Nehru saw the Buddha as one of the earliest exemplars of precisely this intellectual attitude.

But if Nehru drew upon the Buddha to articulate the ethical foundations of democratic citizenship, Ambedkar discovered in Buddhism the philosophical architecture of social emancipation itself. No modern Indian thinker engaged with the Buddha more intensely than Ambedkar. His encounter emerged from a lifelong struggle against caste oppression and social exclusion. Ambedkar was searching for a moral philosophy capable of dismantling hierarchy while preserving individual liberty. He found that philosophy in the Buddha.

For Ambedkar, inequality was not simply an economic condition; it was embedded in social relationships, cultural practices and religious legitimations. Political democracy could not survive if society remained governed by graded inequality. This concern reflected a profoundly Buddhist understanding of human interdependence. Oppression was not merely a moral failure of individuals but a structural condition reproduced through tradition, institutions, and customs. Liberation, therefore, required transforming both consciousness and society.

It is precisely here that Buddhism enters the Constitution, not through explicit religious reference but through constitutional morality. The Constitution nowhere invokes the Buddha, yet many of its deepest commitments echo the ethical universe that Ambedkar believed Buddhism represented: the rejection of inherited hierarchy, the affirmation of human dignity, respect for reason, and compassion as the basis of public life.

Fundamental rights prohibit discrimination and, thus, the abolition of untouchability attacks not merely a social practice but an entire civilisational logic of exclusion. Affirmative action recognises that formal equality is insufficient where historical injustice has distorted opportunity. Moving further, the Directive Principles envision a social order grounded in justice rather than privilege. Constitutional morality itself demands restraint in the exercise of power.

These are not simply legal arrangements. They reflect an ethical conception of society remarkably consistent with Ambedkar's reading of Buddhist philosophy. His final intellectual testament, The Buddha and His Dhamma , completed shortly before his death, reinterpreted Buddhism as a philosophy of democratic society rather than metaphysical salvation. Religion, he argued, should concern itself with relations between human beings; morality must precede theology; and justice must precede ritual.

This interpretation transformed Buddhism into a language of citizenship. Nehru and Ambedkar thus approached the Buddha from different historical experiences. Nehru encountered him as the architect of India's rational civilisation and Ambedkar encountered him as the liberator of India's oppressed. While Nehru emphasised ethical governance, Ambedkar emphasised social revolution. Nehru celebrated the Buddha's intellectual freedom while Ambedkar foregrounded his radical egalitarianism. Yet, reading them after so many decades, it appears that these differences were complementary rather than contradictory. Together, they reveal two indispensable dimensions of constitutional democracy which were inspired by Buddha’s teachings.

This synthesis perhaps explains why the Constitution possesses a moral depth that distinguishes it from many constitutional documents across the world. It does not merely distribute power but it aspires to transform society and seeks a more humane civilisation. This aspiration becomes especially relevant in our own times. Across many democracies, constitutional procedures survive even as democratic culture weakens. Majoritarianism increasingly claims electoral legitimacy while neglecting constitutional restraint. Public discourse is increasingly polarised, with reason yielding to propaganda and compassion mistaken for weakness. These developments reveal a crucial truth that Constitutions alone cannot defend themselves.

Ambedkar and Nehru suggest that constitutional democracy is neither merely a legal arrangement nor simply a political system. It is a way of inhabiting the world, a continuous practice of respecting human dignity, questioning arbitrary authority, extending compassion beyond one's own community, and recognising that no society can remain free while large sections of its people remain excluded.

Perhaps this is why the Buddha continues to speak so powerfully to India's constitutional imagination. His teachings were never confined to monasteries as they belonged equally to the public square and they asked not only how an individual might live ethically but also how a society might organise itself around justice rather than domination. The Constitution gave institutional form to that aspiration of the people: Ambedkar supplied its language of social democracy while Nehru infused it with democratic humanism. Though they never directly engaged each other on this question, together they ensured that the Republic of India would aspire to be more than a State. It would seek to become a moral community, anchored in liberty, equality, fraternity, and the enduring belief that the dignity of every human being is inviolable.

Manoj Kumar Jha is Member of Parliament (Rajya Sabha), Rashtriya Janata Dal

editorials.title: When millet trumped meat
editorials.passage:
Despite the inevitable stiffness that accompanies ceremonial dinners everywhere, many actually looked forward to the ones at India’s Rashtrapati Bhavan. These occasions were famed for their excellence when it came to presenting the best dishes that India had to offer. One has, of course, never heard of either a president who ritually approves the menu, or any prime minister taking an unusual interest in the fare. So it was left to the hospitality wing of the Rashtrapati’s household and the top chef attached to it to decide the dishes in consultation with the external affairs ministry’s protocol division that spelt out the known preferences and the taboos of visiting dignitaries.

Of late, however, it appears that someone with a singular interest in pushing millet and other dishes from western India has been influencing the choice of dishes. As a result, India appeared quite inconsiderate in foisting an aggressive vegetarianism on hapless heads of State at the recent BRICS Summit dinner. This has evoked controversy. The invited presidents as well as a prime minister, crown prince and foreign minister would surely have missed at least one non-vegetarian dish in the menu.

Even a casual look at the list would reveal that the invited heads were from almost totally non-vegetarian countries where beef is the preferred meat. Indian officialdom has banned beef, just as many countries abhor pork, but a health-conscious host could always offer chicken or fish as better options to compulsory non-vegetarians.

One can only visualise the deep disappointment of our honoured guests who scrolled up and down an impressively worded menu but could not locate at least one fish dish — forget meat delicacies. Millet is millet, rather tasteless and tough for most. Could the poorly-equipped metabolic systems of the less fortunate have digested the ‘Millet Pulao’? The other courses, camouflaged in exotic names, comprised paneer (cottage cheese), beans, carrots and dal .

The fare, quite obviously, will not bring a smile to those who have savoured some unforgettable dishes — Kachche Gosht ki Biryani, Dum Pukht Biryani with Sheermal, Tandoori Chicken and Nargisi Kofta — served by the same Rashtrapati Bhavan in the past that did wonders with better-known Indian cuisine. The former prime minister, Manmohan Singh, was a vegetarian but he served non-vegetarian Indian dishes like Chingara Jammu Prawn, Fish with Green Chilli, Kakori Kebabs, Green Chilli Lamb and Mughlai Chicken to Barack Obama in 2010. The then POTUS was so pleased that he scrawled a big thank you note on the menu card. Now that’s hospitality. But what his successor did was force his version of vegetarian food on foreign guests; this is just not done.

One needs to highlight that India is an overwhelmingly non-vegetarian country. Vegetarians outnumber non-vegetarians in just 5 states among 36 states and Union territories. National Family Health Survey-5 found 70.6% of women and 83.4% of men consumed fish, chicken or meat at least occasionally and 45.1% of women and 57.3% of men consumed them sometimes. According to a Sample Registration System baseline survey, vegetarians were in a majority only in Rajasthan (74.9%), Haryana (69.25%), Punjab (66.75%), Gujarat (60.95%) and Madhya Pradesh (50.6%) while every other state had a clear majority of non-vegetarians.

Facts notwithstanding, the ultra-orthodox regime of Uttar Pradesh never misses an opportunity to compel its 53% non-vegetarian population to abjure fish or meat by citing religion or by imposing local bans and restrictions during festivals. Madhya Pradesh and others ape this model.

And herein lies a tragedy. This vegetarian caucus equates its myopic version of ‘pure Hinduism’ with an uncompromising vegetarianism and imposes its dominance over the rest. It ignores the shameful fact that India has the world’s highest number of children with malnutrition — stunting afflicts 35.5% Indian children against the world average of 23.2% while wasting is evident in 19% against a global average of 6.6%. The World Health Organization’s request to serve eggs to counter malnutrition among children as eggs have high nutrient-density, high-quality protein, choline, Vitamin B12 and other nutrients is met with egg bans in this country.

Those who seek to divide Hindus into intractable camps on the basis of diet would do well to read and understand the ‘Social Identity Theory’ of the social psychologists, Henri Tajfel and John Turner. It warns against socio-religious populaces splitting into “in-groups” and “out-groups” and fighting relentless wars. Sunni-Shia extremism and the consequential tragic mass killings are a grim reminder that no group within a religion should impose its values on another.

Jawhar Sircar is a retired civil servant and was a member of the Rajya Sabha

editorials.title: Victims of systemic apathy
editorials.passage:
Fourteen — that is the number of newborn babies who died at Islamabad’s Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences on the morning of August 26 after a fire incident in the neonatal intensive care unit. According to the inquiry report, a localised electrical fault in an air-conditioner supply cable is what probably triggered the NICU fire that led to this heartbreaking tragedy. It adds that while the electrical fault could explain how the fire began, there is no explanation for the failure of successive institutional safeguards that led to the death of 14 medically dependent newborns out of the 15 that were present in the NICU. Only one baby survived. The report says: “Fourteen newborns were lost not because one safeguard failed, but because too many safeguards were absent, weak, delayed or never verified to be working.” The most glaring thing the report highlights is the vulnerability of the nursery where 15 “medically fragile, non-self-evacuating neonates were housed in a 10-bed unit, several dependent on oxygen or respiratory support” while only two doctors and two nurses were immediately available. “No adequately documented, approved, trained and rehearsed nursery-specific fire and neonatal evacuation SOP (standard operating procedure) was demonstrated, nor was a functional automatic smoke detection, alarm or sprinkler system shown to be serving the affected area.” The hospital also lacked a fire-safety no objection certificate.

Today is World Patient Safety Day. The PIMS incident is a stark reminder that such safety mechanisms are mostly absent. PIMS is a hospital that has a huge budget and comes under the federal health ministry. The system has clearly failed the 14 babies who lost their lives. The videos of the mothers, fathers and other family members of these babies were gut-wrenching. Their pain cannot be described. It was a collective failure on the part of the hospital management, the health ministry, the bureaucracy and all those who were directly or indirectly responsible for ensuring the safety of each and every patient in the hospital. Such tragedies are a grim reminder of the callous apathy of our systems.

Another such reminder is the murder of Mir Raza Ali, a graduate of the Institute of Business Administration and businessman, who was found dead in Karachi a day after he went missing on July 28. This case underlines how the system is trying to sabotage the investigation. The Karachi police surgeon, Summaiya Syed, told a judicial commission that she was threatened and followed by men on motorcycles for two days after disputing the findings of the first post-mortem . Originally, it was being alluded that he had committed suicide. His body was later exhumed because Syed found loopholes in the first post-mortem . Instead of praising her, the provincial government was unhappy with Syed for going on television, especially since she made it quite clear that she had shared her findings with top officials but did not get any response. The second post-mortem established that Mir Raza sustained multiple injuries before his death and thus suicide was ruled out. There have been other issues with this case and the way in which the investigation is being stalled or sabotaged by the police and the Sindh government is shocking. Had young people not come out on the streets to protest this murder and had the police surgeon not gone on Shahzeb Khanzada’s programme on Geo News and revealed that she found several loopholes in the first post-mortem , this murder would have been swept under the carpet without any hope of justice or closure for Mir Raza’s family. We still don’t know if they will get justice. But at least there is enough media and public pressure on the authorities now to be accountable in one way or another.

The tragedy at PIMS and the alleged cover-up of the murder of Mir Raza are just two incidents that show us how easily our established systems fail the common people. This is why the ruling elite needs to do something to change how things are. An overhaul and improvements are needed. The ruling elite cannot just go on pretending that these are normal occurrences.

Mehmal Sarfraz is a journalist based in Lahore; mehmal.s@gmail.com

editorials.title: Weak link: Editorial on linguistic diversity and the Centre’s Hindi push
editorials.passage:
The Union government’s emphasis on Hindi is for the best of reasons. On the occasion of Hindi Diwas, the Union home minister, Amit Shah, was at pains to explain this. In multilingual India, Hindi was meant to be just a link language, to enable dialogue and create a sense of affinity among Indian languages. Mr Shah did not forget to say that it would strengthen national unity too; apparently that was the function of a common ‘link’ language. Mr Shah seemed to be countering widespread fears and resentment regarding what is perceived as the Bharatiya Janata Party-led government’s constant efforts to impose Hindi all over the country. He hastened to assert that Hindi is in no way a competitor to other regional languages; it will develop alongside the preservation and the promotion of all of them.

It is unfortunate that Mr Shah’s reassurances are belied by the government’s practices. Central legislations are named in Hindi in spite of complaints that these names are incomprehensible to many Indians. Besides, naming laws in Hindi ignores Article 348(1)(a) of the Constitution which says that all business in the Supreme Court and high courts should be conducted in English. The new three-language formula introduced in Central Board of Secondary Education schools is being seen as a way to force Hindi on non-Hindi-speaking states as two of the languages learnt have to be Indian, one being the mother tongue. Financial incentives are apparently being given to Central government employees to write files in Hindi. Official correspondence, it is alleged, is being written in Hindi even if the receiving official or state does not use the language; a member of Parliament from a non-Hindi-speaking state received a letter written in Hindi with no English version. Instead of strengthening unity, the insidious insertion of Hindi — notwithstanding Mr Shah’s noble declarations — can lead to differences. Language touches the roots of identity; coercion by political force in the sphere of language is a way to suppress diversity and pluralism through cultural insensitivity. The spirit of freedom enshrined in the Constitution celebrates diversity, be it in speech or religion. In a democracy, people should be free to learn and speak the language they wish to; communication between the Centre and the states and between languages will evolve out of the will to communicate, as it has always done.

editorials.title: Two views: Editorial on India’s diplomatic balancing act and its limits
editorials.passage:
‘Strategic autonomy’ — non-alignment in another name? — is being hailed as a potent tool in India’s diplomatic arsenal. The policy has had its success, of course. For instance, this approach has helped New Delhi keep its channel of communication open with nations and blocs that are, in a manner of speaking, the movers and shakers in the sphere of geostrategy. That is not an insignificant success. In a fractured global polity, very few nations retain India’s ability to engage with a wide cross-section of countries involved in mutual competition or conflict. Strategic autonomy’s benefits, its endorsers also argue, are not limited to India. It has enabled nations that pull in different directions to arrive at a precious consensus. At the BRICS Summit, New Delhi’s ability to build bridges was apparent in the engagement between Iran and the United Arab Emirates, two nations located at opposite ends in the West Asia crisis. Three years ago, in the G20 forum, India had similarly smoothened the differences between Russia and Western countries with the help of the capital accrued from its pursuit of strategic autonomy.

But can such consensus lead to the cherry-picking of reality? This is a relevant question. Consider the New Delhi Declaration at the BRICS Summit. In its endeavour to achieve broader consent, it not only made no mention of the warring parties in the war in West Asia but also voiced concerns rather cautiously. Ukraine remained the elephant in the room in the BRICS declaration: Moscow would have minded otherwise. That is not all. Is consensus enough in a world battered — splintered — by conflicts? Engagement should ideally lead to meaningful collective action. That has not been the case and, consequently, the global fires — Ukraine and West Asia are just two examples — continue to burn. When conversation results in inertia, the potency and the principles of a fraternity — in this case BRICS — may come under scrutiny. New Delhi’s role as an enabler of difficult conversations within multilateral groupings is to be appreciated. But conversations between competitors that are the fruits of New Delhi’s strategic autonomy must be followed by interventions that could make a difference. In this, the ace in India’s diplomatic pack of cards is yet to deliver.

editorials.title: Dollar deluge: options for liquidity management
editorials.passage:
India’s external current account deficit (CAD) remains manageable. However, net capital inflows dried up during the last two years, resulting in the RBI losing foreign exchange reserves. The problem was compounded by the US-Iran war since February 28, 2026. Short-term initiatives by the government and the RBI, including reduction of special excise duties on petrol and diesel, liberalisation of external commercial borrowings (ECBs), reduction of net open position by authorised dealers (ADs) and interventions in the forex market, were not enough to arrest the rupee’s depreciation. Both the RBI and government announced a slew of measures on June 5, for further liberalisation of capital account transactions, including limited period offer for dollar mobilisation under special swap schemes.

The RBI made the swap schemes attractive for banks to raise fresh FCNR(B) deposits and swap the foreign currency with the RBI for rupees on a fully hedged basis. Moreover, the RBI exempted these deposits from CRR, SLR, PSL requirements, removed the interest rate ceiling and allowed leveraging against primary dollar deposits, which enabled banks to offer better rates to NRIs.

The RBI wanted dollars. It got so much that it closed its special FCNR(B) swap window a month ahead of the original deadline. By August 31, banks reported $136.37 billion in forex inflows under the dollar-rupee forex swap facility, of which $127.23 billion came through FCNR(B) deposits. The experiment was highly successful, surpassing all previous such attempts.

The rationale for the dollar hunt was straightforward. A stronger foreign-exchange position gives the RBI more room to deal with pressure on the rupee and provides a cushion against external shocks. Foreign portfolio flows can be volatile, while other stable sources of foreign capital were not coming in quickly enough. FCNR(B) deposits offered a relatively quick way to bring in foreign currency, although at a cost.

The more interesting part of the story begins after the swap. The dollars went to the RBI, and equivalent rupees credited to banks. Those rupees can be lent, invested, and used to repay liabilities with a time lag or can be simply parked with the RBI. The RBI data showed a net liquidity absorption of around ₹11 trillion through its LAF window on September 15, 2026. The RBI’s dollar deluge has, rather unexpectedly, created another challenge, managing excess liquidity that came with it. The scale makes the problem harder to ignore. The question is no longer simply whether the RBI should absorb the liquidity. It is how much to absorb, for how long and through which instrument.

The RBI has several options, but each comes with its own trade-offs. The variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) is the most straightforward short-term tool that aligns well with the policy rate. It absorbs surplus funds for a specified period without permanently changing banks’ balance sheets. That makes it useful when liquidity is temporary. If the surplus persists, the RBI will have to keep on rolling over the huge amount under short term VRRR operations. The RBI also went for long term VRRR, but there was a lukewarm response from banks.

Standing deposit facility (SDF) gives banks a safe place to park excess cash with the RBI, but at 25 basis points below the repo rate. As the situation is exceptional, the RBI has the option to temporarily suspend daily fine-tuning, widen the corridor by reducing SDF rate to 3.5 per cent. This will not only activate defunct fixed rate reverse repo but also encourage banks to invest these funds in G-secs until demand for credit picks up. As a result, the benchmark yield may remain under 7 per cent. The RBI may have to tolerate the call rate softening below the repo rate for a while. Banks, reluctant to participate in long-term VRRR or refraining from investment in G-secs, must bear the loss compared to interest offered on deposits.

Option for a hike in CRR does not exist. While CRR is exempted on FNNR(B) deposit, a system-wide increase in CRR would be blunt and could affect banks unrelated to the FCNR(B) inflows. A temporary incremental CRR on the additional deposits mobilised under the swap scheme could violate the very exemption given to such deposits.

The OMO (open market operations) sales can absorb liquidity more durably, but large government bond sales can push yields higher and raise borrowing costs. The RBI has gone for such option and announced ₹1 trillion OMO sales during September 2026. This is not enough, given the size of liquidity surplus. India also has a history of selling G-secs under Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) to deal with large and persistent liquidity arising from capital inflows. On a burden sharing principle, the government should agree as the RBI has already absorbed costs related to swap and VRRR.

Outright forex interventions or FX sell-buy swaps offer another route, allowing the RBI to manage foreign exchange positions and rupee liquidity better. Banks may not buy dollars as their NOP (net open position) is limited to $100 million only. However, banks can buy it on behalf of their customers like oil marketing companies, without violating the NOP guidelines.

The larger point is that absorbing a surplus of this size involves trade-offs. Every instrument has a cost, whether it is paid by the RBI, banks, government, or the bond market. The real choice is which cost is easier to absorb. The RBI should therefore not try to sterilise every rupee simply because it has entered the system.

Some liquidity will naturally move into credit and investments sooner or later. The first task should be to determine how much of the surplus is temporary and how much is likely to persist. In the near term, a combination of 14-day VRRR and SDF can manage the immediate surplus, supplemented by longer-tenor VRRR. If a sizeable portion proves durable, OMO sales, sell-buy forex swap, and eventually G-sec sales under MSS could come into play.

Bhoi is Chief Economic Adviser, and Nair is Economic Research Analyst, AU Small Finance Bank. Views are personal

Published on September 17, 2026

editorials.title: Are foreign resources crucial for growth?
editorials.passage:
A persistent trope in much of the economic development literature is that significant catch-up by lower income countries necessarily requires additional foreign savings to add to domestic savings, so as enable higher investment rates to generate faster growth. This led to the related argument made especially from the 1990s onwards, that countries should deregulate their financial sectors and particular liberalise cross-border financial flows, to attract more foreign investment, either as equity or loans.

This was so widely accepted by multilateral economic organisations and by policymakers across most developing countries that it became almost axiomatic, and resulted in waves of financial liberalisation that swept the Global South over the past few decades. We know now that this has created many problems for developing countries, from greater constraints on domestic economic policy making to extreme volatility in financial flows with associated domestic financial problems, greater vulnerability to crises driven by global shocks and macroeconomic policies in the major advanced economies, to external debt stress in many countries. But did it at least achieve the aim of transferring financial resources from North to South?

One way of assessing the macroeconomic outcome is to look not at net financial flows but at the domestic savings and investment rates in developing countries in the period of more open capital accounts. If external capital (of whatever kind) is positively contributing to investment, we expect investment rates to be higher than savings rates. Here we examine data from 2001 onwards, when external financial openness was very widely practised in most developing countries.

As Figure 1 shows, throughout this period, over the past quarter century, aggregate savings rates across all low and middle income countries were higher— and in some years, quite significantly higher — than domestic investment rates. In effect this amounts to a net transfer of resources abroad, from countries that can ill afford this because they still need to increase investment for their development project and to meet the climate challenge.

It could be argued that this aggregate result reflects the disproportionate role of China, which has maintained current account surpluses and high savings rates that have generally been much higher than investment rates throughout this period. Over this entire period, the savings rate in China was 45.4 per cent of GDP, while the investment rate was 40.6 per cent. Given China’s large and growing weight in this group of countries, this would certainly have affected the aggregate numbers.

Therefore it is also worth looking at a sub-group of such countries — the lower middle-income countries that are often also referred to as “emerging markets” while lower income countries are classified as “frontier markets”, largely because of the different financial investor perceptions they tend to be associated with.

Figure 2 shows the average for the sub-group of lower middle income countries (which includes India) and finds a different time trend. Yet even for these countries, the picture since 2001 has been mixed, with several years of savings rates being close to or slightly higher than investment rates. It is only after 2016 that there seems to be a clear trend of domestic savings rates falling below domestic investment. Also, it is not clear from this whether the countries in this group were able to benefit from foreign savings to actually increase their growth rates more than before.

Therefore, it is worth looking at the experience of some individual countries. We consider here three of the more well-known “success stories” in developing Asia: Malaysia (which is an upper middle income country now very close to achieving high income status); Indonesia, which is seen as a fast-growing economy; and Vietnam, which has grown rapidly on the basis of a manufacturing export boom largely driven by Chinese investment.

These country cases are instructive. Malaysia had very high rates of both savings and investment in the 1990s, which changed dramatically after the Asian Crisis of 1997-98 after which investment collapsed. Figure 3 shows that it continued to have high savings rates leading up to the Global Financial Crisis, more than double the investment rates, which had fallen and remained low. The savings rate fell thereafter, but remained significantly higher than the investment rate, such that Malaysia has been a capital exporter throughout this period.

Similarly, Indonesia (Figure 4) also had savings rates higher than investment rates for almost all years over this period, making it a net capital exporter, despite its greater need for investment.

The most striking case may be that of Vietnam as shown in Figure 5. The country became an exporting powerhouse largely based on foreign investment, but even in this relatively short period, switched to becoming a capital exporter after 2011. Since then, the gap between rising domestic savings rates and stagnant or falling investment rates has only widened.

Figure 6 provides another way of looking at the role of foreign finance, now not in terms of the net macroeconomic effect, but in terms of the share of domestic investment financed by foreign finance in one way or another (through equity or loans). The most striking feature is the rapid decline evident over the past decade, not only for all developing countries, but for all categories as well as for every single developing region. For emerging and frontier markets, where the ratios were already small, they have approximately halved to reach tiny shares of domestic investment.

What all this suggests is the need for foreign finance for economic development has been vastly overstated. Supposedly “successful” countries have become capital exporters well before their development project is anywhere near completion, while over the past decade, lower and middle income countries as a whole have had much smaller shares of foreign finance in domestic investment. It is clearly time to move beyond this problematic assumption.

Published on September 17, 2026

editorials.title: Decoding Coforge saga
editorials.passage:
The abrupt resignation of OP Bhatt, Chairman of the Board of Coforge Ltd, and the subsequent resignation of DK Singh, Chairman of the Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC), has raised some fundamental questions on the process and approach to the annual Board evaluation procedure adopted by companies.

From available press reports, it has emerged that the internal audit carried out on the Board evaluation process found that some parts of the evaluation reports were made available only to Bhatt and Singh and were not shared with other Board members. It has also been reported that the Chairman of the Board secured a low rating, which was also not shared with the NRC and the Board.

The remit of this piece is limited to the efficiency and the rigour attached to the Board evaluation procedure and does not seek to draw conclusions on what exactly went wrong and who is responsible for the same. Lessons from Coforge have to be digested and necessary corrections made in the larger context of good corporate governance.

Most companies undertake this exercise with the seriousness as mandated by the regulators. The coverage extends to evaluation of each Board member, the Board as a whole and the Chairman of the Board. The onus of this exercise is with the Chairman of NRC with the support of external agency. A detailed presentation is finally made to the Board, which also highlights critical comments and areas of improvements. The objective is to enhance the overall quality of deliberations at the Board and, more importantly, to send a strong message that every individual is accountable and evaluated, including the Chairman of the Board.

By no means is this exercise a mere tick of the box. The details of the evaluation is also part of the records for verification by the regulatory agencies. In all fairness, the details of evaluation of each member of the Board is, to some extent, linked to the minutes of Board and committee meetings, which capture the essence of what each Director stated at the meeting. Of course, in virtual meetings, the contribution of each Director is also on record since the meetings are recorded. Coforge is a professionally managed and a widely held listed company and not a promoter-driven company. Hence, by design, the process of Board evaluation has to satisfy the twin tests of objectivity and fairness. Unconfirmed reports have indicated that individual differences of opinion among Board members have found their way in the Board evaluation and individual rating. If so, it is unfortunate to say the least. Board congeniality and collaboration is a sine qua non for effective corporate governance.

Views can be expressed at meetings, but individual differences have to be sorted out outside the Board room. Differences should never be part of Board evaluation process since it destroys the fabric of objectivity.

An interesting aspect is that the issue surfaced, thanks to the internal audit highlighting a clear lapse of withholding key information to the Board. This is a classic case of an audit finding highlighting gaps in the overall governance framework, particularly in the context of information being withheld to the Board.

History is replete with instances of corporate governance failures where information relating to key transactions have not been fully disclosed to the Board. Coforge is a rare case of the some aspects of Board evaluation not being shared with the Board.

There are two key takeaways from the Coforge episode. Withholding information to the Board is a serious lapse that needs to be nipped in the bud. All key managerial personnel, who are the custodian of information and reports, must ensure that irrespective of compulsions, information flow to the Board has to be complete.

The process of Board evaluation has to be serious enough to ensure that facts are captured and, more importantly, fairness must be ensured. The worst fallout of the Coforge saga is that corporates may, from now on, spend a disproportionate amount of time on the Board evaluation process. The need of the hour is to strike the right balance between compliance and business.

The writer is a chartered accountant
