They turned out to be followers of Gurmeet Ram Rahim, a self-styled godman who had set up a religious organisation called the Dera Sacha Sauda, which had grown politically influential on the back of its following among the Dalits of Punjab and Haryana.

Ram Chander Chhatrapati died of his injuries a month later at the age of 52. In the run-up to the murder, he had been relentlessly publishing stories about rape allegations against Ram Rahim.

The godman’s driver later told investigators that he had overheard him instructing his followers to murder the journalist. But the driver dithered in court, taking years to eventually stand by his testimony. It took 17 years for Ram Rahim to be convicted for Ram Chander Chhatrapati’s murder.

In March, the Punjab and Haryana High Court overturned the 2019 conviction, taking the view that the driver’s word could not be relied upon.

Anshul Chhatrapati is unfazed by the setback. He has filed an appeal in the Supreme Court, which will hear his petition in November, just months before Punjab votes in the state assembly elections. Behind bars, Ram Rahim has continued to wield political influence: in the nine years he has spent in jail after being convicted on rape charges in 2017, he has been released on parole 17 times, often coinciding with elections.

“We are not going to stop,” said Anshul Chhatrapati. “The struggle is not over.”

It is a struggle that has reshaped his life. He was in college when his father was murdered. Pursuing justice through the legal system meant he could not attend classes and eventually had to drop out. Fighting the powerful godman came with its own risks: an armed guard of Haryana Police shadowed him for decades. The security cover extended to his entire family.

“My children haven’t had a normal childhood,” said Anshul Chhatrapati, now in his mid-40s. “For a better part of their childhood, going out for them only meant heading to school and back.”

But he has no regrets. “My father would have been very proud of me,” he said. “This struggle has made a man out of me.”

Like thousands of families in North India, Anshul Chhatrapati’s family traces its roots to Pakistan. After Partition, his grandfather had tried to build a new life. “Once he settled in India, the refugees were allotted agricultural land to derive their livelihood,” he recalled. “At that time, Sirsa’s land was not cultivable at all but our ancestors had no choice.”

Born in 1950, Ram Chander Chhatrapati, however, was a non-conformist. He did not have much interest in farming. “His true calling was writing and activism,” Anshul recalled. “He loved reading newspaper editorials, Munshi Premchand and Lenin.”

After he completed his college education in Haryana, Chhatrapati moved to Delhi. “My father spent quite a long time in Delhi with Swami Agnivesh, a follower of Arya Samaj,” Anshul said. The Arya Samaj is a Hindu reform movement. His parents felt he was wasting time and brought him back home to get married, said Anshul. “They felt it was the only way to make him serious about life and his share of land.”

After his marriage, Chhatrapati studied law and began practising at Sirsa district court. The family was also supported by the income from his share of the agricultural land. “But he was not satisfied being a lawyer,” said Anshul.

In 2002, Ram Chander Chhatrapati quit the legal profession and revived an old newspaper registered in his name under a new title – an evening daily called Poora Sach, the complete truth.

In May 2002, a three-page letter written to Atal Bihari Vajpayee, who was the prime minister then, began circulating in Sirsa. A female disciple of Gurmeet Ram Rahim Singh had written the letter alleging that he had raped her. The letter, which was also copied to senior officials in Punjab and Haryana, mentioned that she was not his only victim.

On May 30 that year, Chhatrapati published a two-column front page story about the letter in his newspaper. He did not mention the name of the Dera where the incident had taken place or the guru accused of rape, but he followed the story very closely. Anshul said the anonymous letter had been published by national newspapers but there had been no follow-up reports on it.

Lekh Raj Dhot, Chhatrapati’s friend from his lawyer days, said the journalist had a “passionate” temperament. Everyone told Chhatrapati not to write against the Dera as they could harm him, but that did not deter him, said Dhot. “His psyche was different. There was no fear in him.”

Panicked by the circulation of the letter, there were numerous incidents around Sirsa that year where Dera followers targeted men accused of circulating the letter. “A couple of Xerox shops, accused of making copies of the letter, were vandalised by Dera followers,” recalled Anshul. “My father continued to file stories on these incidents but we had no idea that he had been receiving threats from the Dera henchmen.”

In July 2002, Chhatrapati wrote to the Sirsa superintendent of police, detailing the intimidation he was facing at the hands of Dera. “He mentioned a phone call in which he was threatened and how some suspicious people outside his office had created an atmosphere of terror for him and his staff,” said Anshul.

In September 2002, the Punjab and Haryana High Court took cognisance of the anonymous letter and sought a report from the district sessions judge of Sirsa. In a report to the high court, Sirsa district judge MS Sular recommended a probe by a central investigation agency. On September 24, 2002, the Punjab and Haryana High Court ordered the the Central Bureau of Investigation to investigate the rape allegations.

According to Anshul, his father had managed to get the copies of the correspondence between the two judges. “He filed stories on all these developments.”

The Dera Sacha Sauda soon approached the high court, seeking a stay on the directions for a CBI probe, but the court dismissed its application. “On October 23, 2002, my father published a story about that,” said Anshul. “The next evening, he was shot five times outside our home by two men from Dera Sacha Sauda.” Chatrapati died a month later in a hospital in Delhi.

Anshul recalled his father as someone who could not look away from wrongdoing, even if he knew the consequences could be harmful. “He used to tell his friends that if someone ever dared to hurl anything at him, it wouldn’t be a shoe but a bullet,” said Anshul. “And he will take that bullet on his chest.”

In its initial statement on Chhatrapati being shot at, the Sirsa police had described the incident as a “property dispute.”

However, the police had to discard that theory immediately. “There’s a police post near our house and one of the shooters had run towards the post in panic,” recalled Anshul. “He ran directly into the policemen who were rushing towards the commotion.”

The shooter was identified as Kuldeep Singh, a Dera follower from Faridkot Punjab. The other shooter was his cousin Nirmal Singh, who was arrested a few days later. “The police recovered a walkie-talkie from their possession which was registered in the name of Dera Sacha Sauda and a pistol which was licensed in the name of Krishan Lal, a manager at the Dera,” Anshul added.

According to Anshul, the arrest of Kuldeep Singh on the spot was a fundamental piece of evidence in establishing the role of the in Dera Sacha Sauda his father’s murder. “We would have cried all our life about the Dera’s involvement but who would have trusted us?”

All the three accused whose names surfaced in the preliminary investigations were arrested by the Sirsa police, but Chhatrapati’s family was not satisfied. “The Sirsa police had avoided naming the Dera chief as the main conspirator behind the murder even when my father had given a statement on his death bed while being hospitalised,” said Anshul.

In early 2003, the family filed a petition before the Punjab and Haryana High Court, seeking a Central Bureau of Investigation probe.

Another development helped Chhatrapati’s family.

Three months before Chhatrapati’s killing, Ranjit Singh, a Dera follower and former manager of Ram Rahim, was shot dead on July 10, 2002, at his native village in Haryana’s Kurukshetra district. Ranjit Singh’s family had also approached the Punjab and Haryana High Court, demanding a CBI inquiry in his murder. “The high court clubbed both these petitions together.”

On November 10, 2003, the High Court ordered the CBI to investigate the journalist’s murder case anew. The CBI registered a first information report in Chhatrapati’s murder on December 9, 2003.

But the CBI could not start its investigation as some female disciples of the Dera Sacha Sauda challenged the High Court’s order in the Supreme Court. In 2004, the Supreme Court stayed the high court’s CBI probe order . “It took the Supreme Court a year to dispose of the Dera’s petition and uphold the high court’s order.”

This would become a permanent feature in the more than two-decade-long battle to pin down the role of Ram Rahim in Chhatrapati’s murder. “From day one, we wanted the investigation agency to go to the root of the murder which was the Dera chief Gurmeet Singh,” said Anshul. For Chhatrapati’s family, that meant a constant vigil on the developments in the case. “Every time we felt there were attempts to shield him, we approached the court. Once the court ruled in our favour, the sect would approach the Supreme Court.”

While these legal skirmishes took a lot of time and frustrated the family, they did not give up. “How could we face the world if Chhatrapati’s family gave up the fight against evil?”

In July 2007, the Central Bureau of Investigation filed a chargesheet against Dera chief Ram Rahim, his manager Krishan Lal and the two shooters, Kuldeep Singh and Nirmal Singh. The agency charged all four with murder and criminal conspiracy. Nirmal Singh and Krishan Lal were also charged under the Arms Act.

In its separate chargesheet filed the same year, the agency established that the Dera chief suspected Ranjit Singh of circulating the anonymous letter which accused the godman of raping female disciples in the sect’s premises. This was the same letter which Chhatrapati had written about extensively in his newspaper between May 2002 until his murder in October, 2002.

A key witness who helped the CBI pin down Ram Rahim was Khatta Singh, a long-time driver of the self-styled godman.

Khatta Singh had recorded a statement before the agency in 2007 in which he deposed that he had witnessed Gurmeet Singh ordering Krishan Lal, Nirmal Singh and Kuldeep Singh to “eliminate” Chhatrapati so that “he may not write against Dera Sacha Sauda in future.” Singh had recorded the same statement under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before a judicial magistrate in Chandigarh.

This testimony was crucial but Khatta Singh turned hostile during the trial in 2012. According to the CBI, Khatta Singh was under “tremendous pressure” due to “threats.”

Khatta Singh also happened to be a witness in the murder of Dera manager Ranjit Singh which was being investigated separately by the CBI.

It was only after the conviction of Gurmeet Singh for raping his two female disciplines and subsequent imprisonment in August 2017 that Khatta Singh changed his mind.

Nearly three weeks later, Khatta Singh moved an application before the CBI court in Panchkula, seeking to be re-examined as a witness in the trial of Chhatrapati’s murder. However, the trial court dismissed Singh’s application, forcing him to move the Punjab and Haryana High Court in 2018.

In January 2019, the Chhatrapati’s family found a semblance of justice. The CBI special court convicted Ram Rahim and three others for the journalist’s murder and sentenced them to life imprisonment.

Seven years later, the Punjab and Haryana High Court acquitted Ram Rahim in the journalist’s murder case in March. The court said “absolutely no reliance can be placed on a witness like Khatta Singh”. It observed that Khatta Singh had chosen to stay silent for a number of years after the incident and “kept on tossing from one side to the other like a ping pong ball.”

Earlier, in May 2024, the High Court had also acquitted Ram Rahim in the murder case of his former manager and follower Ranjit Singh. The Dera chief, however, remains in jail, serving a 20-year-long imprisonment for rape.

Ram Chander Chhatrapati was survived by his wife, two sons and two daughters. As the eldest child, it fell upon Anshul to take charge of the legal battle against his father’s murderers. Anshul was just like any other college student then, but his father’s death inspired him. “The struggle for justice became the purpose of my life,” he said.

“All my life, every stranger felt like a threat to me,” said Anshul. “But that never stopped me from going out and facing the world.”

“The common perception is that law took its course and eventually punished the culprit,” he continued. But the reality was different. “From day one, there were attempts to keep away Dera’s involvement in the murder. That’s why we had to fight from the very first step and follow the case’s development obsessively.”

This left him with no time to finish college. “During all these years, I had tried to restart my education but I couldn’t continue because there would be a development in the case and I had to act accordingly, meet lawyers and approach courts, etc,” he noted.

The family’s agricultural land proved to be a safety net. Anshul earns his living from farming even though he looks like a corporate employee, dressed in stylish clothes and shiny shoes.

A soft-spoken man, he joked as he wondered what his life might have been like, had his father not been murdered. “I was recently telling my daughter that we both should pursue our graduation together,” he chuckled.

editorials.title: Kancha Ilaiah Shepherd writes about the teacher who urged him to study despite his Shudra status
editorials.passage:
One morning, school teacher Rajalingam came to my house when my mother was sprinkling buffalo and cow dung water around our house. He had on trousers, a bush shirt and rubber slippers on his feet. What attracted me most were his clean white feet with blue slippers. His long face with curly black hair made me think that he was an unusual man from an unknown world. He was entirely different from the men I had seen so far. What he wore itself was a kind of fancy dress in my village. When he came home, my mother hurriedly left her work, put out a cot and spread a bedsheet on it while he stood at a corner politely.

This could have been in May or early June of 1960. My mother requested him to sit. For the first time in her life she heard someone address her politely, “Kattammagaru, you must send your two sons to the school.” I clearly remember my mother dressed in a red and blue sari and a black blouse. She heard him attentively. I stood at a distance, listening to their conversation carefully. My mother first resisted him. She said, “Ayya, education does not go well with my family. My elder son, Mallaiah, died after we sent him to a private teacher. I do not want these two beggars to die. As my atta (mother-in-law) says, Saraswati (Hindu goddess of education) will kill our children if they are sent to school.” He tried to convince her that these were superstitions. Saraswati would bless them and give them education, he said. My mother would not budge, “Saraswati teaches the children of the bapanollu and komatollu but she becomes a devil when it comes to our children. She will not allow our children to read and write. She will kill them. This is how my elder son died.”

Then she bought each one of us a slate and a few chalks. She took my brother Kattaiah and me to school, met Rajalingam and told him, “Ayya … Saaru…they will come to school, perekkiyyi” – register their names. His eyes glowed like electric bulbs… two more fellows to keep his job alive in the village. He opened a register and asked her when each one of us was born and approximately gave us a date, month and year of birth. We had no janma namam or ritual recording of birth time and date, but a school namam (a birth record was created in the school in our names). Now I own that date, month and year as God-given, though I was not a God’s child in terms of the Indian caste system. In the school, I became a being with a name that was written on a paper with a future of my own. A date, a month and a year has entered into the logbook of history along with my name. So also for my brother Kattaiah. But my twin younger sisters were not fortunate enough to get into a school. The Police Patel sent his second daughter, Chandrakala, to school as he had no sons. They too had to stop as they were married when they finished Class 5.

After independence, school had its role in that process. But before the school was founded, the Police Patel had bought a radio which was big news in the village. I remember that when I first went to school, I wore the clothes that I did when I grazed the buffaloes: a small panche – loincloth, folded and tucked between the buttocks, and a half-shirt to cover the upper body. I had bulky silver bangles on my wrists and small gold earrings in my ears. A child wearing such things was a symbol of well-being within the caste and village culture. Even now, my ears have those holes. We never knew what knickers or underpants were. Quite unlike the frog that jumped out of the well, I jumped out of the large world of fields and cattle, full of free movement, into a small well called school. A feeling of being confined haunted me all along, especially sitting with folded legs on the small leaf mats that we carried along with us from 10 am to 4 pm with a one-hour lunch break.

Right from the age of five, my brother and I had begun to have a life in the wilds. I had tended cattle, sheep and goats. In the world of the fields, one does not focus on just one thing. One sees many things at a time. You observe the cattle or sheep with their different behaviour – moving, running and eating. At the age of seven, I was a master of the flock. We were woken up in the early morning. By then the cattle would have been untied from the poles. We used to have some buffaloes for milk, some cows to procreate, and bulls for tilling the land. We had two pairs of cattle to till the land. They would get fed well first, followed by the milking buffaloes. We would walk behind them, inhaling all the dust that they raised and crushing the dung they excreted on the way.

The most interesting period of cattle grazing was the early monsoon time when rain had given birth to green grass all around the village. When the dusty summer ended and the monsoon season began, it was pleasant and green grass would begin to sprout all around the village. The beauty of green grass spreading out like a carpet around the village would give us energy to run all around. We used to play in it, sleep on it. Kotha neeru, rainwater, formed ponds all around the village. That was a really pleasant playtime. Cattle grazing in the early monsoon, in the yet-to-be tilled wet lands that made a green carpet, was fun. Exactly at that time would school start. The feeling of all playtime taken away by a jail-like school used to linger in my mind. School was boring; the field was thrilling.

Excerpted with permission from A Shudra Life: An Autobiography, Kancha Ilaiah Shepherd, South Side Books.

editorials.title: Under PM Modi’s leadership, India’s foreign policy has grown confident in its own skin
editorials.passage:
Any assessment of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s impact on India’s foreign policy is necessarily incomplete, because unlike politics, foreign policy has a longer arc and an even longer period of gestation. That said, one advantage we have with this prime minister is his longevity. Modi is already India’s longest-serving PM in terms of continuous elected tenure.

One more advantage is that Modi is a generational leader and a global statesman, with a unique blend of vision, timing and influence. He has, over the course of a 12-year journey as the occupant of India’s most powerful office, repeatedly given examples of his leadership skills in some exceptionally trying times for India and even the world.

Over this past decade, India’s engagement with the wider world has undergone a quiet yet profound transformation. A reflexively cautious approach has given way to self-assured maturity, and its regional footprint has extended to the global stage.

India has steadily transitioned into a rule-shaper — actively contributing to norms, institutions and mechanisms that govern the international system. Whether in stitching together global coalitions on clean energy and disaster resilience, championing digital public infrastructure as a template for emerging economies, or bridging global ‘North’-‘South’ divisions, New Delhi is no longer merely participating in global conversations and accepting rules. It is helping set the agenda.

And Modi is central to this transformation. What sets him apart as one of the world’s tallest leaders today is not merely political longevity, but a rare combination of decisive domestic authority and exceptional diplomatic dexterity.

In an era marked by fractured geopolitics and big-power contestation, Modi commands a degree of mandate and policy stability that few global peers possess. This political capital has allowed him to approach foreign policy with greater long-term strategic clarity than short-term electoral anxieties.

On the world stage, Modi has demonstrated an unusual ability to build genuine rapport across geopolitical and ideological divides. No other world leader can share an embrace with Israel’s prime minister and walk hand in hand with the Iranian president almost simultaneously. Modi is equally at home in the capitals of the West, the halls of the Kremlin, the monarchies of the Gulf, and the summits of developing nations across the Global South.

The prime minister’s ability to shape global outcomes was on display during India’s G20 presidency. Heading into the 2023 edition in New Delhi, deep divisions over the war in Ukraine had led many observers to predict that a joint communiqué was impossible.
Modi led India in navigating the fault lines to deliver a unanimous Leaders’ Declaration on the very first day. Three years later, as the chair of the 18th Brics Summit, India again pulled off the seemingly impossible by successfully achieving a consensus, leading to the unanimous adoption of the Brics New Delhi Declaration.

More importantly, Modi had used India’s G20 presidency to shift global attention away from geopolitical wrangling towards shared human concerns. India launched the Global Biofuels Alliance and demonstrated how its own scalable digital public infrastructure could empower developing nations to achieve rapid financial inclusion.

The same instinct was evident at the recently concluded Brics Summit. Led by Modi, India steered the agenda by driving a collective shift for the Global South from “rule-takers to rule-shapers”, an effort that included a 10-proposal global governance reform roadmap to democratise international decision-making and diversify the financial architecture. In so doing, Modi ensured that Brics as a bloc remains ‘non-Western’ rather than ‘anti-Western’, safeguarding India’s strategic flexibility and sparing the Global South the pressure of ‘picking a side’.

The international order faces active conflict zones in Eurasia and West Asia, alongside an uneasy relationship between the US and China. Amid this turbulence, the prime minister has systematically enlarged Bharat’s strategic space.

With the US, India has cultivated a strategic partnership of great depth, driving collaborations in critical domains such as defence and security, critical and emerging technologies, and supply chains such as the Pax Silica Initiative. And he has done so while navigating crippling challenges thrown at the bilateral relationship by a mercurial Donald Trump.

At the same time, New Delhi has maintained its historic relationship with Moscow, ignoring Western pressure while prioritising domestic energy security. With China, India has demonstrated strategic patience and resolve. Following the 2020 border tensions, New Delhi stood firm, maintaining that normalisation of ties was impossible without peace and mutual disengagement along the frontier. That determination has eventually led to a thaw in ties despite structural rivalry.

As a leader, what sets Modi apart is his ability to see the larger picture. He has spent considerable time and effort improving India’s relationship with its immediate neighbours (with the exception of Pakistan) while taking the long view. The aim, as External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar pointed out in an address in 2023, is to create a benign neighbourhood. In his words, “a benign neighbourhood doesn’t happen by itself. It happens when the largest country in the neighbourhood invests in the rest of the neighbourhood.”

In practice, that meant that when Sri Lanka was pushed to the brink of sovereign default and societal collapse, India stepped in with over $4 billion in food, fuel and financial lifelines without attaching predatory conditions. In Nepal, India has funded hundreds of high-impact community development projects, directly building schools, hospitals and rural roads. India’s power ministry, for instance, has just approved the urgent export of up to 654 megawatts of electricity daily to Nepal to help it recover from the devastating flash floods that crippled its power infrastructure.

Even in Afghanistan, despite political upheaval, India has consistently delivered grain, life-saving medicines and winter supplies directly to the people. Modi’s foreign policy is anchoring neighbouring economies directly to India’s growth engine, turning regional proximity into a shared advantage.

Beyond the immediate land borders, Modi has engineered a dynamic expansion of India’s influence in its extended neighbourhood. To the East, the ‘Act East’ policy is deepening institutional, physical and digital ties with Asean nations, extending India’s strategic horizon into the wider Indo-Pacific maritime domain.

To the West, he has overseen a truly transformative relationship with the Gulf before Trump’s reckless war against Iran created difficulties for everyone. This engagement enabled connectivity frameworks like the I2U2 grouping and the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor.

To the North, India is intensifying engagement with Central Asia. Modi became the first Indian prime minister to visit all five Central Asian republics. Apart from geopolitical balancing, increased engagement with this region is crucial for India’s energy and mineral security and for bypassing transit blockades.

To the South, through the SAGAR doctrine and its broader evolution into MAHASAGAR, India views the ocean as an integrated space of shared prosperity. By deploying naval assets for rapid HADR assistance and investing in sustainable marine economies, India has established itself as the preferred security partner and first responder across the Indian Ocean basin.

This diplomatic outreach is backed by a complete reimagining of statecraft. For a leader who was taunted as “provincial” and “bereft of knowledge of statecraft” by elites, Modi has fundamentally redefined security, taking it far beyond military preparedness and counterterrorism to include economic, technological and health resilience.

In this framework, true sovereignty requires shielding the nation from weaponised supply chains and technological dependencies. Modi has woven economic diplomacy into foreign missions, driving export promotion and diversification of vital components.

Technological security has been placed at the centre of international negotiations, ensuring India is not left out of artificial intelligence and semiconductor ecosystems. For instance, on Wednesday, Modi chaired a ‘Semiconductor Roundtable’ with CEOs in New Delhi, as part of a major push to move India from building foundational capabilities to scaling up across the global chip value chain.

In the realm of health, the Vaccine Maitri initiative demonstrated how humanitarian values and strategic capability can deliver millions of life-saving doses to vulnerable nations during a global crisis, establishing India as an indispensable first responder.

The fullest expression of Modi’s geopolitical vision can be found in India’s increased footprint in Africa. India’s diplomatic engagement and developmental assistance in Africa have expanded exponentially under his tenure. Altogether, 18 Indian embassies have been opened in Africa alone, making India’s diplomatic network on this continent one of the world’s most extensive.

As Jaishankar has observed, “A global footprint means being present in Latin America, being present in the Caribbean, being present in Central America, engaging with the Pacific Islands, doing something in Mongolia, going to Norway.”

Taken together, these achievements reflect a foreign policy that has grown confident in its own identity. By combining civilisational connect with strategic realism, Modi has guided India away from ideological stiffness into strategic flexibility.

India today stands as a steadying and moderating force in an unpredictable world — a trusted partner, neighbour, active first responder, a vital hub for global technology and supply chains, and a leading power shaping the rules of a rapidly changing international order.

(Views expressed in the above piece are personal. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: It takes two to tango: The Dragon and Elephant must dance for global peace
editorials.passage:
The contemporary global order is fractured by two devastating, overlapping conflicts: the Russia-Ukraine war and the US-Iran war. These conflicts are no longer confined to being regional disputes; they have mutated into systemic crises threatening global energy supplies, economic stability, and international security. As the pre-eminent economic powerhouses and demographic giants of Asia, India and China hold a unique, historically significant obligation to lead the world toward peace.

While bilateral friction has long defined their relationship, the existential threats of these dual wars dictate that Beijing and New Delhi must put aside their border disputes to forge a joint diplomatic front. By leveraging their collective strategic autonomy, economic clout, and shared regional platforms like Brics and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO), India and China should intervene to end these endless hostilities.
Fractured Global Economy and Energy Markets
The most immediate and pragmatic reason for Sino-Indian cooperation is the profound threat these wars pose to their domestic economic growth. China is the world’s largest crude importer, drawing roughly half of its supply from West Asia. The US-Iran war directly imperils the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint through which Asian energy lifelines flow. Similarly, India's rapid development relies heavily on stable, affordable energy. Though India has cushioned its economy by purchasing discounted Russian oil amid the Ukraine war, an uncontained conflict in West Asia, coupled with persistent Western sanctions severely disrupts maritime trade and fuels runaway inflation.

If major Asian powers speak with one voice, the rest of the world will listen. Renowned economist Jeffrey Sachs noted that a combined demand from India and China to “end the war” holds unparalleled weight. If the fighting continues, the prolonged economic costs will be catastrophically absorbed by Asia.
Dangerous Polarisation of Great Powers
The dual wars have accelerated a highly volatile realignment of global powers, forcing both Beijing and New Delhi into uncomfortable diplomatic tightropes. For India, the prolonged Russia-Ukraine war has pushed its historical partner, Moscow, into an asymmetrical economic and political dependence on Beijing. This dynamic shifts the balance of power in Asia, complicating India's security landscape. Concurrently, Washington's aggressive stances and transactional policies — such as imposing tariffs on Indian exports over Russian oil ties — expose the limits of relying solely on Western alliances.

For China, a protracted war involving the United States in West Asia may temporarily distract Washington, but it risks a catastrophic global escalation that undermines Beijing’s long-term economic integration projects. By working together, India and China can neutralize the pressure to “choose sides”. A united Asian consensus would provide a buffer against the destabilizing actions of an unpredictable United States and a desperate Russia, preserving the multipolar world that both Asian powers desire.
Minilateral Diplomacy via Brics and SCO
India and China possess the exact diplomatic architecture needed to broker peace, yet they underutilise it due to mutual distrust. As key architects of the SCO and the expanded Brics bloc, they sit at the same table as the primary combatants and their closest allies. Iran and Russia are both members of these blocs, making them uniquely receptive to Asian diplomacy.

Currently, differences between India and China have hamstrung these institutions from forging a unified stance on the West Asia crisis. If Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese President Xi Jinping synchronise their strategies, they can transform Brics and the SCO from passive talking shops into powerful conflict-resolution mechanisms. They can collectively pressure Moscow to accept a realistic exit strategy in Ukraine and leverage their deep ties with Tehran to facilitate a ceasefire with the US and Israel.

The solution to the modern world's geopolitical fires cannot be found on the battlefield. As Prime Minister Modi aptly remarked at the SCO Summit, humanity must move “from endless war to the end of war”. Neither the United States nor Russia can unilaterally dictate a peaceful global order anymore. For India and China, cooperation is no longer an idealistic choice; it is an absolute strategic necessity. By leveraging China’s unparalleled economic advantage over Moscow and Tehran alongside India’s robust diplomatic credibility with both the West and the Global South, these two Asian titans can stop the global slide into total war. In doing so, they will not only protect their own economic futures but will permanently secure their status as the rightful, responsible leaders of the 21st century.
Conclusion
India and China do not need to agree on every geopolitical issue to recognise a shared fire when it burns near their homes. By setting aside differences and demanding a halt to the US-Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars, both nations can fulfill their roles as leaders of the Global South and secure a safer, more stable world. India and China must unite their diplomatic influence to demand an end to the US-Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war because these ongoing conflicts severely threaten both nations’ energy security and economic stability. As global heavyweights, New Delhi and Beijing possess the collective economic and political weight to push warring parties toward the negotiating table.

Working together is no longer just a diplomatic choice; it is an urgent necessity for Asian and global survival. Cooperation on global peace can also help India and China improve their own bilateral relations. As both nations work to stabilise their border regions and maintain economic growth, partnering for global stability offers a clear path forward.

(The writer is a retired Indian diplomat and had previously served as ambassador in Kuwait and Morocco and as consul general in New York. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: When wildlife goes viral: The troubling human obsession with animal celebrities
editorials.passage:
Every once in a while, an animal comes along that captures the collective imagination of human beings and, for a moment, becomes something akin to a superstar in the people-world. The latest debutante to join that line-up is Jimothy, Seattle’s renowned raccoon that is capturing headlines across the world.

First spotted two months ago, this round-spined, neckless animal has since gone viral on social media and his fame has spread not only across the US but globally as well. Now his every movement is carefully mapped, multiple global news outlets are running stories on him and Seattle City Hall has already christened 2026 the summer of Jimothy. There have been the usual marketing spin-offs too and enough merchandise to earn him a spot on the roster of all-time famous fauna.

Jimothy isn’t the only animal to earn merchandising and marketing deals because of his sudden popularity. When it comes to the cuteness quotient, Tasmania’s Neil the seal is a clear winner, his antics fetching millions of likes and comments on social media. He routinely visits the coast of Tasmania, wreaking havoc on local infrastructure before returning to the sea. This year was no exception and just as Jimothy was gaining visibility in Seattle, Neil the seal finished his summer chaos and returned to the sea in July 2026. There are hundreds of videos and reels of him online and a dedicated fan following that has grown consistently over the years.

Perhaps the most acclaimed animal ever to capture human imagination was Paul the octopus. From his lair in an aquarium in Oberhausen (Germany), Paul accurately predicted the outcome of a number of football matches during the FIFA World Cup 2010. So seriously did soccer fans take this clairvoyant mollusc that his predictions were live-streamed and fans of rival teams that lost a game even sent hate mail and death threats.

The world was divided into Paul lovers and Paul haters, with Iran announcing that he was a symbol of Western weirdness while Russian and Kazakh bookmakers offered insane money to buy him. As the world gawked, performance, ad and brand deals poured in and he even got an agent. Then the tourney came to an end. Three months later, he was dead. A decade and a half on, his memorial is buried somewhere and the world has moved on to another gawk-worthy animal.

Animals finding sudden fame or notoriety isn’t new. Sadly, human interest is seldom either long-standing or particularly beneficial for the animal in question. A good example is what happened to the first elephant to ever migrate to America.

Transported by ship from Calcutta, the poor animal reached New York Harbour after an arduous four-month journey on April 13, 1796, and was craned to the shore.

People paid between 25 and 50 cents to see it, and such was the craze that even George Washington, the American president, went to have a dekko. After its gawk debut, the elephant was sold to a circus where it became a sellout act for 20 years.

Ultimately, though, this story came to a sad end when the elephant was shot dead by a bigoted local farmer. Reason: he thought the idea of spending money to see a circus was just plain sinful. So much for celebrity status.

Human beings are good at cherry-picking random animals to obsess over depending upon the mood of the moment. That the human world rarely spares a thought for all the other species that we share the earth with only makes this sudden spotlight even more tragic. Animals don’t understand celebrity. They are not being intentionally cute or clever or just plain strange. Most often, they are simply surviving in a world that gives them little room to do so.

Very often, the reason they pop up on our radar is because our habitats clash with theirs. Neil the seal is an example. That this naughty five-year-old male elephant seal should keep coming back to the Tasmanian coast is pure biology. He was born there and returns for his ‘haul-out’ or rest period. What’s not normal is that he is the only seal to come to that beach. Completely isolated during his haul-out, far away from other breeding colonies of elephant seals and surrounded by humans, his chaotic behaviour, which we find cute and funny, is pure survival instinct. He is doing what a young male elephant seal does to establish his dominance over his environment. His behaviour is natural. Our gawking less so.

One look at how we behave on big cat safaris tells the story. Every time a tiger or lion is spotted, cameras zip out and tourists take thousands of pictures of the animal. That celebrity often gets the animal poached at worst. At best, it sends out a signal that its territory has been encroached upon by humans.

Spinning an urban myth around an animal is perhaps not the worst that Homo sapiens can do to flora and fauna. After all, folk traditions and myth-making have taught human beings to forge a live-and-let-live relationship of some kind with the animal world. But given the far more common instances of animal cruelty, it’s not ideal either. The animal world deserves our respect and protection. Both of which translate to space. Sadly, that’s not something a viral presence on social media guarantees.

(Nandini Sen Gupta is a freelance writer and author of several books. Views expressed in the above piece are personal and solely those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect Firstpost’s views.)

editorials.title: NRIs Gain, India Pays: What Will Record FCNR(B) Inflows Cost the Nation?
editorials.passage: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) reported provisional forex inflows through Foreign Currency Non-Resident Bank—or FCNR(B)—deposits of $127.23 billion until 31 August 2026. This is when the scheme closed a month earlier than the pre-announced 30 September. The FCNR(B) inflows are clearly much higher than what the RBI had planned in June. The apex bank is bearing the entire hedging/foreign exchange depreciation cost of FCNR(B) deposits received by Indian banks.The FCNR(B) inflows are indeed humungous—confirmed by the fact that India’s foreign currency assets (FCAs) climbed to $648.68 billion (and total forex reserves, including gold, to $785.71 billion) on 4 September 2026 against $541.12 billion (total forex reserves $672.59 billion) on 19 June 2026, an increase of more than a hundred billion dollars.Now that the FCNR(B) deposits have landed, they will have to be serviced and repaid. These deposits carry very high rates of interest, including forex depreciation cost. There are other costs as well. So, what are actual costs of FCNR(B) deposits? Who will bear it—banks, the RBI, government, or the nation? Will it impact the RBI's surplus transfer to the government adversely? And how will the rupee exchange rate behave—favourably or otherwise?India’s Dollar Economy (Part 1): Net FDI Fell to Zero – Yeah, It’s True!The FCNR(B) deposits from the NRIs were raised by the banks—public sector, private sector, and foreign banks operating in India. The RBI decided to absorb all hedging costs for the banks. It took the dollars received in FCNR(B) deposits from banks against rupees and promised to give back equal amount of dollars on deposits' maturity at the same exchange rate—and free them from other associated costs (maintaining zero interest earning cash reserve ratio or capital charge). This encouraged the banks to rake up the FCNR(B) deposit interest rates to their rupee deposits. FCNR(B) dollar deposits, which paid about 3 percent interest before the scheme was launched, have received 6-6.5 percent interest. FCNR(B) deposits of $127 billion for about 4.5 years (about 50 percent deposits are for five years), will cost roughly $17.5 billion in additional interest cost (at about 3 percent extra interest) or about Rs 1.75 trillion (at Rs 100 per dollar exchange rate) or about Rs 35,000 crore every year in cash. Actual rupee cost of interest would be much higher as the hedging cost of interest paid in dollars is not absorbed by the RBI.It was expected that the rupee would appreciate as the RBI would get more firepower to defend the rupee. The fact that more than $100 billion came in through the FCNR(B) deposits should have led to rupee appreciating to 90 to a dollar. The experience of the last four months, however, belies this. The rupee was at 95.79 to a dollar on 4 June 2026. On 5 June, the day RBI announced the scheme, it strengthened to 94.95 to a dollar. It has traded in a range-bound manner since then—appreciating to 94.36 on 26 June and 94.49 on 4 September; and depreciating to 96.35 on 16 July, 96.57 on 24 July, and 95.70 pm 21 August. On 11 September, it traded at 95.56 to a dollar. It did not appreciate at all. On 14 September, it nearly touched 96 to a dollar.The pressure on rupee will resume now. Total reserves of $800 billion are no better in firepower strength than $700 billion of reserves. Continuously high current account deficit (thanks to oil as well) and adverse inflows in capital account will take its toll. That it would be Rs 100 to a dollar by the end of financial year 2026-27 is a near certainty.If we consider 5 percent annual depreciation from now on (not an unreasonable bet), the rupee would be close to 120-125 to a dollar in 2030 when the bulk of FCNR(B) deposits mature. If we take additional cost of Rs 25 per dollar of FCNR(B) deposit (over 95 at which these have been received), foreign exchange depreciation cost would be about Rs 3.18 trillion for $127 billion of deposits. The total bill of additional cost for the FCNR(B) deposits is thus about Rs 5 trillion (Rs 1.75 trillion + Rs 3.18 trillion).Why the Rupee Remains Under Pressure Despite RBI's Foreign Inflow SchemesThe NRI depositors have all gains and no risk. They will get much higher interest (at least 1.5 percent) over the dollar deposits if kept in the US, Europe, or West Asia. They are earning extra return on their own deposits if they had taken advantage of the leverage (about 15 times) offered by Indian banks (by taking loans at 0.5/1 percent lower interest from their foreign branches). There is no foreign exchange risk for them and no risk of default. It is balle balle for them. Indian banks cut it very fine and may not really gain anything. They jumped on the FCNR(B) bandwagon for two reasons: First, they wanted to please their bosses—the RBI and the government—by making the scheme a grand success. Second, they had reasoned out that if they could get the FCNR(B) deposits in rupee even at about half a percent lower effective interest cost than their rupee deposit costs, it would benefit them.The banks had assumed that they would be able to lend their newfound resources at higher rates of interest. The experience of the last few weeks suggest that their assumptions were not robust. In the absence of their ability to lend the FCNR(B) resources at remunerative rates, the liquidity in the banking system has gone through the roof—crossing Rs 10 trillion. The banks cannot invest their extra liquidity in VRR and other facilities offered by the RBI, as they offer lower interest than their cost of FCNR(B) deposits. They are not putting these resources in government securities either. The banks may eventually lend this money. In the interregnum, however, they suffer a negative carry. Considering all factors, it seems quite clear that the banks do not bear any part of Rs 5 trillion extra cost bill but their expectations of making any good profits will not materialise: they might end up suffering some cost. The RBI has strange incentives in the game. It has to deploy the dollars received with the foreign central banks, International Bank of Settlement or invest in foreign governments’ securities. As the RBI keeps its foreign investments and deposits highly liquid, the interest it would earn on its investments is lower than the interest which the banks pay on FCNR(B) deposit. There is thus a net loss of interest on the round-trip of foreign-sourced FCNR(B) deposits ending as the RBI’s deposits with foreigners. As it is not specifically accounted for the RBI, it is the national loss. An additional Rs 1.75 trillion interest cost/loss is formally on the banks' book and impacts their net interest margin (NIM). However, the banks are putting up a brave face by counting the FCNR(B) flows at 6/6.5 percent as incremental resource, which would increase their profits even if NIMs go down.The case of hedging cost/rupee depreciation cost is weird as the RBI’s rupee profits go up when the rupee depreciates. A dollar received by the RBI at Rs 90 gives Rs 10 of profit when the RBI sells or values it at Rs 100 later. Thus, even if the rupee depreciates to 125 to a dollar in 2030, the RBI’s balance sheet would not suffer any loss. Its FCAs would be valued at Rs 125 to a dollar. The loss RBI would generate on giving FCNR(B) dollars at Rs 95 in 2030 would be no loss as its dollar deposits/investments, against would have become equal to Rs 125. In the unlikely situation of the rupee not depreciating in the next four years, the RBI does not bear any cost as there was no depreciation.  Thus, the Rs 3.18 trillion of foreign exchange loss will be suffered by the nation as costlier dollar raises the cost for everyone—importers, oil purchases, debt service and everything else. RBI's 'Debt Wish' Will Make India's Forex Reserves More Precarious Going ForwardThe FCNR(B)-induced foreign currency reserves increase of about $100 billion, in the absence of any likelihood of strengthening rupee, does not adversely impact the likely dividends to the government from the RBI. As the nation absorbs the additional cost of Rs 5 trillion while rupee depreciates, the RBI would keep paying good, if not hefty, dividend to the government.(Subhash Chandra Garg is the Chief Policy Advisor, SUBHANJALI, and Former Finance and Economic Affairs Secretary, Government of India. He's the author of many books, including 'The $10 Trillion Dream Dented, 'We Also Make Policy', and 'Explanation and Commentary on Budget 2025-26'. This is an opinion piece, and the views expressed above are the author’s own. The Quint neither endorses nor is responsible for the same.)
